1.pericope_label: The blessing of Moses, and the shining forth from Sinai

schools.summary: Gill says the first verse is the general title to the chapter, and that Moses is called the man of God as being raised up of God and eminently qualified by him for the work he was called to, and inspired by him to say what follows; it is a title given to prophets, Onkelos paraphrasing it, Moses the prophet of the Lord, and Aben Ezra observing that this is said to show that he blessed Israel by a spirit of prophecy, which he did a little before his death, on the very day of it. Of the second verse he says Moses relates what in some things he was an eye and ear witness of, and in others was inspired by the Spirit of God to deliver, concerning the future case and state of the several tribes, after observing the common benefit they all enjoyed by having such a law given them in the manner it was. Of the love he says it was shown to the people of Israel, of which the giving of the law in such a glorious manner was an instance and a distinguishing blessing which other nations were not favoured with; how much more, he adds, is the love of God shown to his spiritual Israel by giving them his Gospel and, above all, his Son to be their Redeemer. These he embraces in his arms and in his bosom, as the word here signifies, admitting them to great nearness and familiarity with him. Calvin says the bitterness of the Song was seasoned, as it were, by this palliative, the blessing being like sugar, wherein Moses left a testimony with respect to God's future and perpetual grace, as if depositing an inestimable treasure in the hands of the people. For as God, after the deliverance of his people and the giving of the Law, renewed the covenant which Jacob had testified of and proclaimed, so Moses was as it were their second father, to ratify anew its blessings, lest the memory of them should ever be lost; and in order to beget confidence in his benedictions he commences by magnifying his vocation before he proceeds to them. Of the coming from Sinai Calvin says Moses reminds them that he is setting before them a confirmation of the covenant which God had made with them in this Law, and that it is nothing different from it, for this connection was of exceeding efficacy in establishing the certainty of the blessings, provided only the Law was duly honoured, since nothing was better adapted to confirm the grace of God than the majesty displayed in the promulgation of the Law. Some, as Calvin conceives improperly, translate it, God comes to Sinai, whereas Moses rather means that he came from thence, when his brightness was made manifest; and by way of ornament the same thing is repeated with respect to Seir and Paran. Of the peoples he says that if it be preferred to apply this to the Gentiles, the sentence must be resolved thus, that although he loves all human beings, still his saints are honoured with his peculiar favour in that he watches over their safety; but it is more correct, Calvin says, to expound it as referring only to the children of Abraham, whom he calls peoples because, on account of the multitude into which they had grown in their several tribes, they might be reckoned as so many nations. Since the Hebrew particle signifies prolongation of time, the sense will be very satisfactory that, although the descendants of Abraham were divided into various races and might therefore seem to be separated, they were still one people.

Henry says the first verse is the title of the chapter, and that it is a blessing: in the foregoing chapter Moses had thundered out the terrors of the Lord against Israel for their sin, a chapter like Ezekiel's roll, full of lamentation and mourning and woe; now, to soften that, and that he might not seem to part in anger, he here subjoins a blessing and leaves his peace, which should descend and rest upon all those among them that were the sons of peace. Thus Christ's last work on earth was to bless his disciples, like Moses here, in token of parting as friends. Moses blessed them as a prophet, a man of God; and it is a very desirable thing, Henry notes, to have an interest in the prayers of those who have an interest in heaven.

Clarke summarises the chapter as a prophetical blessing delivered to the children of Israel, with an introduction, then prophetic declarations concerning Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Gad, Dan, Naphtali and Asher in order, closing with the glory of the God of Jeshurun and the glorious privileges of his true followers. Of the love he says this is the inference which Moses makes from those glorious appearances, that God truly loved the people, and that all his saints, the people whom he had consecrated to himself, were under his especial benediction; and that in order to make them a holy nation God had displayed his glory on Mount Sinai, where they had fallen prostrate at his feet with the humblest adoration, sincerely promising the most affectionate obedience, and had there commanded them a law which was to be the possession and inheritance of the children of Jacob. Wesley says Moses is said to bless them by praying to God with faith for his blessing upon them, and by foretelling the blessings which God would confer upon them; and that he calls himself here the man of God, that is, the servant or prophet of God, to acquaint them that the following prophecies were not his own inventions but divine inspirations. Of the children of Israel he notes that the several tribes are meant, only Simeon being omitted, either in detestation of their parent Simeon's bloody carriage, for which Jacob gives that tribe a curse rather than a blessing, or because that tribe had no distinct inheritance but was to have its portion in the tribe of Judah. The Lord came, he says, means to the Israelites, manifesting himself graciously and gloriously among them, beginning at Sinai where the first appearance of God was, and so going on with them to Seir and Paran; he rose up means he appeared or showed himself, as the sun does when it rises; and from Seir means from the mountain or land of Edom, to which place the Israelites came, and from thence God led them on towards the land of promise, and then gloriously appeared for them in subduing Sihon and Og before them. Of the love Wesley says the sense is that this law, though delivered with fire and smoke and thunder, which might seem to portend nothing but hatred and terror, yet in truth was given to Israel in great love, as being the great means of their temporal and eternal salvation; yea, he embraced the people and laid them in his bosom, so the word signifies, which speaks not only the dearest love but the most tender and careful protection. All God's saints or holy ones were in thy hand, that is, under God's care to protect, direct and govern them; and these words are spoken to God, the change of persons between his and thy being most frequent in the Hebrew tongue.

Ellicott says the title man of God is here used for the first time, its counterpart being found in the next chapter, where Moses the servant of Jehovah died; the more any man is a servant to Jehovah, he says, the more is he a man of Elohim to his fellow-men, and after Moses it is Elijah and Elisha who are more especially described by this title in the Old Testament. On the words before his death he quotes Rashi: and if not then, when should he? Of the second verse he gives the rendering, Jehovah came from Sinai, and dawned upon them from Seir; he shone forth from mount Paran; and there came from the ten thousands of holiness, from his right hand, a fire of law for them. The appearance of God on Sinai, he says, is described as a sunrise: his light rose from Sinai, and the tops of the hills of Seir caught its rays, while the full blaze of light shone on Paran. He came with ten thousands of saints, Ellicott says flatly, is a mere mistranslation, since the preposition is from, not with. Of the third verse he gives the connection thus: from his right hand went a fire, a law for them, that is, for Israel; loving the peoples also, that is, all who should hereafter become his people; all his saints are in thy hand, the hand of him who spake on Sinai and now speaketh from heaven; and they are seated at thy feet, the feet of the same heavenly Prophet; every one shall receive of thy words. Or possibly, he adds, the last clause means that he, that prophet, will take of thy words, that is, of Moses' words, and we know he did so. Keil says that on comparing the blessing of Moses with that of Jacob we should expect at the very outset that, if the blessings of these two men of God have really been preserved to us and are not later inventions, their contents would be essentially the same, so that the blessing of Moses would contain simply a confirmation of that of the dying patriarch and would be founded upon it in various ways. This is most conspicuous in the blessing upon Joseph, he says, but there are also several other blessings in which it is unmistakeable, although Moses' blessing is not surpassed in independence and originality by that of Jacob, either in its figures, its similes or its thoughts. Of the third verse Keil renders, yea, nations he loves; all his holy ones are in thy hand, and they lie down at thy feet, they rise up at thy words; the phrase for loving nations is the subject placed first absolutely, and the nations or peoples, he insists, are not the tribes of Israel here, any more than in the preceding chapter or in Genesis.

debates: Whom he loved: Keil renders it, yea, nations he loves, and insists the peoples here are not the tribes of Israel at all; Calvin states the Gentile reading and rejects it, holding it more correct to refer the word only to the children of Abraham, called peoples because their tribes had grown into so many nations; Ellicott takes them for all who should hereafter become his people; Clarke, Gill and Wesley keep to Israel

Whether the Lord came with or from ten thousands: Ellicott calls the received rendering a mere mistranslation, since the preposition is from and not with, and renders, there came from the ten thousands of holiness, from his right hand, a fire of law for them

Whether he came to Sinai or from it: Calvin says some translate it improperly as God comes to Sinai, whereas Moses means that he came from thence when his brightness was made manifest, and Wesley reads the three places as stages of one journey rather than one appearance

What relation this blessing bears to Jacob's: Keil sets it up as a test of authenticity, that if both were really preserved and are not later inventions their contents should be essentially the same, and finds this most conspicuous in the blessing on Joseph, while granting that Moses is not surpassed by Jacob in independence or originality
outliers: Calvin's figure that the blessing was like sugar seasoning the bitterness of the song
Calvin's description of Moses as the people's second father, ratifying the covenant anew lest its memory be lost
Ellicott's rule that the more a man is servant to Jehovah, the more he is a man of God to his fellow-men
Ellicott's alternative reading of the last clause, that the prophet will take of Moses' words, and we know he did so
Henry's comparison of Moses parting with a blessing to Christ's last work of blessing his disciples
Rashi's comment quoted by Ellicott, that if not before his death, when should he bless them?
Wesley's note that Simeon alone is omitted, whether for the parent's bloody carriage or for want of a distinct inheritance

4.pericope_label: The law an inheritance, the king in Jeshurun, Reuben and Judah

schools.summary: Gill says the law was of God, of his enacting, a declaration of his will with his authority stamped upon it, he being the lawgiver, which lays men under obligation to regard it; but it was delivered to Moses, and by him to the children of Israel, on whom he urged obedience to it, so that it is said to come by him and is sometimes called the law of Moses. Of the king in Jeshurun he says the meaning is, in Israel, or over the people of Israel: either God, as Jarchi has it, for the government of the Israelites was a theocracy and their laws were immediately from God, and by him they were guided and directed in all things, so that when they were importunate for a change in their government and to have a king over them they are said to reject the Lord, that he should not reign over them; or Moses, as Aben Ezra and Maimonides and others have it, who under God had the civil government of the Hebrews. Both may be received, Gill says. Of Reuben he says the meaning is that the tribe should continue and not be extinct, though it should not excel, because of the sin of its progenitor; and it may have a special regard to the preservation of their families on the other side Jordan while they passed over with their brethren into Canaan, which Jacob by a spirit of prophecy foresaw and prayed for. All the three Targums, Gill notes, refer the words to a future state. Of Judah he says the supplement, this is the blessing, is made in the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem, though Aben Ezra thinks it refers to what goes before, that the same thing prayed for Reuben belongs also to Judah, that he should live and not die, perhaps in the wars in which that tribe would be engaged. Calvin says that what Moses had declared respecting the glory of God and the excellency of the Law he now applies to his own person, since it was his purpose to establish the authority of his own ministry; in order to prove the certainty of his mission he boasts that he was appointed by God to be the teacher of the people, and that not for a brief period but throughout all ages, for by the word inheritance the perpetuity of the Law is signified. He then claims for himself the royal supremacy, not because he had ruled after the manner of kings, but that the dignity of this high office might add weight to his ministry. Of Judah Calvin says Jerome has faithfully given the sense, this is the blessing, although it is not actually expressed. It might at first sight appear inconsistent that some abatement should be made from the splendid and abundant blessings which had been promised to the tribe of Judah; this, however, is by no means the case, for the inviolable decree respecting the supremacy of Judah is not thus altered, but Moses merely reminds them how difficult of accomplishment it would be. Jacob had declared, as if speaking of a peaceful dominion, that his brethren should praise him and that his father's children should bow down before him.

Henry says that though Reuben had lost the honour of his birthright, yet Moses begins with him, for we should not insult over those that are disgraced, nor desire to perpetuate marks of infamy upon any, though ever so justly fastened at first. Moses desires and foretells the preserving of this tribe: though a frontier tribe on the other side Jordan, let it live, and not be either ruined by its neighbours or lost among them; and perhaps he refers to those chosen men of that tribe who, having had their lot assigned them already, left their families in it and were now ready to go over armed before their brethren.

Clarke says that of Reuben, though his life and his blessings had been forfeited by his transgression with his father's concubine and in his rebellion with Korah, let him not become extinct as a tribe in Israel. It is very usual in the Scripture, says Mr Ainsworth as Clarke quotes him, to set down things of importance and earnestness by affirmation of the one part and denial of the other, as in, thou shalt die and not live; that they may live and not die; I shall not die but live; that we may live and not die; and cursed be the day. Of Judah Clarke says that though the word blessing is not in the text it may be implied from the first verse, but probably the words he spake are those which should be supplied: and this he spake of Judah, Lord, hear the voice of Judah; that is, says the Targum, receive his prayer when he goes out to battle and let him be brought back in safety to his own people. Let his hands be sufficient for him means, let him have a sufficiency of warriors always to support the tribe and vindicate its rights, and let his enemies never be able to prevail against him. Wesley says Moses speaks of himself in the third person, which is very usual in the Hebrew language, and that the law is called their inheritance because the obligation of it was hereditary, passing from parents to their children, and because this was the best part of their inheritance, the greatest of all those gifts which God bestowed upon them. He was king in Jeshurun means Moses was their king, not in title but in reality, being under God their supreme governor and lawgiver; and when the princes and people met together for the management of public affairs, Moses was owned by them as their king and lawgiver. Of Reuben he says that though Reuben deserved to be cut off or greatly diminished and obscured, according to Jacob's prediction, yet God will spare them and give them a name and portion among the tribes of Israel and bless them with increase of their numbers. All the ancient paraphrasts, Wesley notes, refer this to the other world, so far were they from expecting temporal blessings only: let Reuben live in life eternal, says Onkelos, and not die the second death; let Reuben live in this world, say Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum, and not die that death which the wicked die in the world to come. Of Judah he says God will hear his prayer for the accomplishment of those great things promised to that tribe, which implies the delays and difficulties Judah would meet with, that would drive him to his prayers, and with success; bring him unto his people means, when he shall go forth to battle against his enemies and fall fiercely upon them, bring him back with honour and victory to his people, to the rest of his tribe who were left at home when their brethren went to battle, and to his brethren the other tribes of Israel.

Keil renders the fourth verse, Moses appointed us a law, a possession of the congregation of Jacob; and he became King in Jeshurun, there the heads of the people assembled, in crowds the tribes of Israel. The God who met Israel at Sinai in terrible majesty, out of the myriads of holy angels, who embraces all nations in love and has all the holy angels in his power, so that they lie at his feet and rise up at his word, gave the law through Moses to the congregation of Jacob as a precious possession, and became King in Israel. Of Reuben he says the blessings upon the tribes commence with the sixth verse: let Reuben live and not die, and there be a number of his men. The rights of the first-born had been withheld from Reuben in the blessing of Jacob; Moses, however, promises this tribe continuance and prosperity. The words, and let his men become a number, Keil says, have been explained in very different ways, and the noun in this connection cannot bear the sense commonly assigned it. Of Judah he says the blessing is introduced with the formula, and this for Judah, and he said: hear, Jehovah, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people; with his hands he fights for him; and help against his adversaries wilt thou be. Judah, from whom the sceptre was not to depart, is mentioned before Levi as the royal tribe. Ellicott quotes Rashi on Reuben, that live means live in this world and not die means not die in the world to come, so that his misdeed should not be remembered; Rashi also notices the juxtaposition of this record with the sentence that the sons of Jacob were twelve. Reuben was not cut off, Ellicott says, but he was disinherited, and his father's blessing had so much in it of disapproval that Moses' prayer for him was not unnecessary. Of the clause, and let not his men be few, he says the sentence is difficult, and that the Septuagint inserts Simeon, let Simeon be many in number, but that there is no need for this. Of Judah he says the words which follow are a kingly blessing, hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people; in other words, when we think of the Lion of the tribe of Judah, thy kingdom come. Rashi reminds us, Ellicott adds, of the many prayers in Old Testament history which were heard from Judah's lips: the prayers of David and Solomon, of Asa and Jehoshaphat, of Hezekiah against Sennacherib, and we may add of King Manasseh and Daniel the prophet, were all the voice of Judah; and the last line of Old Testament history is a prayer of Judah by the mouth of Nehemiah, remember me, O my God.

debates: Who was king in Jeshurun: Gill reports Jarchi for God, since the government was a theocracy, and Aben Ezra and Maimonides for Moses, who under God held the civil government, and receives both; Wesley and Calvin take it of Moses, Calvin as a claim advanced to establish the authority of his own ministry; Keil takes it of God

Whether the two clauses on Reuben speak of one world or two: Clarke explains the form from Ainsworth as a common Hebrew idiom of affirming one part and denying the other, where Wesley reports that all the ancient paraphrasts referred it to the other world, Onkelos giving life eternal against the second death, and Gill and Ellicott confirm the same from the Targums and Rashi

What to do with the clause about Reuben's numbers: Keil says it has been explained in very different ways and that the noun cannot bear its usual sense here, while Ellicott reports that the Septuagint solves it by inserting Simeon, let Simeon be many in number, and judges the insertion unnecessary

Whether Judah's blessing is diminished: Calvin raises the objection that some abatement seems made from what Jacob had promised and denies it, since the decree of Judah's supremacy is unaltered and Moses only reminds them how difficult its accomplishment would be, where Wesley reads the same difficulty as what would drive Judah to prayer
outliers: Ainsworth's idiom, quoted by Clarke, of affirming one part and denying the other, as in, I shall not die but live
Ellicott's reading of the blessing as a kingly one, so that thinking of the Lion of Judah we say, thy kingdom come
Henry's rule that we should not insult over the disgraced nor perpetuate marks of infamy, however justly fastened at first
Onkelos's rendering, reported by Wesley, let Reuben live in life eternal and not die the second death
Rashi's tally, quoted by Ellicott, of the prayers heard from Judah's lips, ending with Nehemiah's remember me, O my God
Wesley's note that Moses speaks of himself in the third person, as is very usual in Hebrew
Wesley's reason for calling the law an inheritance, that its obligation passed from parents to children

8.pericope_label: The blessing of Levi: Urim and Thummim, teaching, and the tithe

schools.summary: Gill says that both the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem make Moses speak here of the tribe of Levi. Of the words about father and mother he says some understand them of the high priests, who according to the law were not to defile themselves or mourn for a father or mother; or rather, as others, of their having no respect to relations in judgment, but determining all causes that came before them according to the law of God and the rules of justice and equity in the most impartial manner, without regard to the nearest relations, and he compares what Christ, the antitype of Levi, says. Of the teaching he says the priests and Levites, being dispersed among each of the tribes and having cities allotted to them, taught the people the laws, statutes and ordinances of the Lord, moral, civil and ceremonial. Of the substance he says it lay in tithes and firstfruits, for the priests and Levites had no share in the division of the land, unless this can be understood of the cities and suburbs given them, or of houses and fields devoted, or rather of their cattle, for whose use they had suburbs appointed them, since in husbandry and merchandise they were not employed; some render the word an host or army, their service being a militia or warfare, and Jarchi refers the clause to the Hasmonaeans or Maccabees, who were of this tribe. Calvin says this qualification, or modification, of the harsher sentence of Jacob was introduced not only for the sake of the tribe of Levi but rather of the whole people. Jacob had said that Simeon and Levi were brethren, that instruments of cruelty were in their habitations, and that his soul should not come into their secret nor his tongue be united to their assembly; assuredly their descendants might have been discouraged, or at least might have been regarded contemptuously, when a patriarch and the founder of their race had thus abominated them. In the person of Aaron, Calvin says, an example is set before all the Levites for their imitation: first, he is said to have renounced his own flesh and blood in order that he might be more disencumbered for obeying God, and in fact it is necessary that all the pastors of the Church should put off their earthly affections, which would otherwise often keep them back from devoting themselves entirely to God. Aaron is said to have bid farewell to all his family that he might be at liberty to lay himself out for God, and Christ now requires the same thing of his disciples, that sons should forget their fathers. Of the prayer for Levi's substance Calvin says it appears to have been intended tacitly to provide against the poverty which awaited the Levites, if God had not supplied them with food from some other source besides the produce of the soil, for they were deprived of a share in the general inheritance and God alone was their property; lest therefore their condition should be painful to them, Moses offers them consolation and bids them expect from God abundance for their support, promising that his blessing shall stand them in stead of the most redundant produce.

Henry says that in blessing the tribe of Levi Moses expresses himself more at large, not so much because it was his own tribe, for he takes no notice of his relation to it, as because it was God's tribe. The blessing of Levi has reference first to the high priest, here called God's holy one, because his office was holy, in token of which Holiness to the Lord was written upon his forehead. Moses seems to acknowledge, Henry says, that God might justly have displaced Aaron and his seed for his sin at Meribah, which might be very remarkable, and which God might have had an eye to in conferring the priesthood upon him.

Clarke says that of Levi the holy one means Aaron primarily, who was anointed the high priest of God and whose office was the most holy that man could be invested with; therefore Aaron was called God's holy one, and the more especially so as he was the type of the most holy and blessed Jesus, from whom the Urim, all light and wisdom, and the Thummim, all excellence, completion and perfection, are derived. God contended with Aaron as well as with Moses at the waters of Meribah, Clarke notes, and excluded him from the promised land because he did not sanctify him there. Of the words about father and mother he says there are several difficulties here: some think they are spoken of the tribe of Levi, others of all the tribes, others of the Messiah; but several of the interpretations founded on these suppositions are too recondite, and should not be resorted to till a plain literal sense is made out. He supposes the whole to be primarily spoken of Aaron and the tribe of Levi, the law having strictly enjoined that if the father, mother, brother or child of the high priest should die, he must not mourn for them. Of the teaching he says this was the office of the Levites, to teach by their significant service and typical ceremonies the way of righteousness and truth to the children of Israel, and that God bears testimony to their faithfulness by the prophet Malachi, whose words about the covenant of life and peace and the law of truth in his mouth are a sufficient comment on the text. Of the substance he says the blessing of God to the tribe of Levi was peculiarly necessary because they had no inheritance among the children of Israel and lived more immediately than others upon the providence of God; yet, as they lived by the offerings of the people and the tithes, the increase of their substance necessarily implied the increase of the people at large, since the more fruitful the land, the more abundant would the tithes of the Levites be, and thus in the increased fertility of the land the substance of Levi would be blessed. Wesley says the Thummim and the Urim are the Lord's by special institution and consecration, and by them he understands the ephod in which they were put, the high priesthood to which they were appropriated, and withal the gifts and graces signified by them and necessary for the discharge of that high office; these shall be with thy holy one, that is, with that priest whom thou hast consecrated to thyself and who is holy in a more peculiar manner than all the people were, so that the priesthood shall be confined to and continued in Aaron's family. Of the words about father and mother he says the sense is, who followed God and his command fully and executed the judgment enjoined by God without any respect of persons; and they kept thy covenant means that when the rest broke their covenant with God by that foul sin of idolatry with the calf, that tribe kept themselves pure from that infection and adhered to God and his worship. Of the substance he says the prayer is because Levi has no inheritance of his own and therefore wholly depends upon God's blessing; the work of his hands means all his holy administrations, fitly so called because a great part of the service of the Levites and priests was done by the labour of their hand and body, whereas the service of evangelical ministers is more spiritual and heavenly. He prays thus earnestly for them, Wesley adds, because he foresaw that they who were to teach and reprove and chastise others would have many enemies, and because they were, under God, the great preservers and upholders of religion.

Keil renders the blessing, thy right and thy light is to thy godly man, whom thou didst prove in Massah and didst strive with him at the water of strife; who says to his father and his mother, I see him not, and does not regard his brethren, and does not know his sons: for they observed thy word and kept thy covenant. This blessing, he says, is also addressed to God as a prayer, the Urim and Thummim being that pledge given to the high priest. In these temptations Levi had proved itself a holy one, although in the latter Moses and Aaron stumbled, since the Levites had risen up in defence of the honour of the Lord and had kept his covenant, even with the denial of father, mother, brethren and children; and the words, who says to his father, relate to the event narrated in Exodus, where the Levites drew the sword. Of the following verse Keil gives, they shall teach Jacob thy judgments and Israel thy law, they shall put incense before thee and whole burnt sacrifice upon thine altar; and then, bless, Lord, his substance, and accept the work of his hands, smite through the loins of them that rise against him and of them that hate him, that they rise not again. Ellicott says that next to Joseph this tribe has the largest share in Moses' last words, as we might naturally expect, it being his own tribe, and that the character of the priest is the principal subject. The blessing may be paraphrased thus: let thy Thummim and thy Urim, the chief high-priestly ornaments, be ever with some saintly man of thine, like him whom thou, Israel, didst tempt in Massah and with whom thou didst strive at the waters of Meribah, Moses' own departed brother Aaron being alluded to, for the people murmured against them both in both places; like him, Eleazar or Phinehas, who said to his father and to his mother, I have not seen him. Of the substance Ellicott says this petition is consistent with the enactment that Levi should have no land, but that a blessing on his substance means a blessing to the whole land of Israel, since Levi's substance was Israel's tithe; the chief work of his hands was mediatorial for all Israel, and the acceptance of this work was essential to the welfare of the whole race. On the prayer to smite through the loins of them that rise against him, Ellicott says Rashi refers to the great war begun by the Asmonaeans, Mattathias the father of the Maccabees having been a priest of the sons of Joiarib from Jerusalem.

debates: Why Levi receives so long a blessing: Ellicott says it is what we might naturally expect, the tribe being Moses' own, while Henry says expressly that it is not so much because it was his own tribe, since he takes no notice of his relation to it, as because it was God's

Who the holy one is: Clarke and Henry take it of Aaron, Clarke adding that he was the type of Christ from whom the Urim and Thummim derive their light and perfection, while Ellicott splits the reference, letting Massah point back to Aaron and the renouncing of kindred forward to Eleazar or Phinehas, and Wesley reads it as settling the priesthood in Aaron's family

Of whom the words about father and mother are spoken: Clarke lists the tribe of Levi, all the tribes, and the Messiah as the proposals, calls several of the interpretations built on them too recondite to be resorted to before a plain literal sense is made out, and settles on Aaron and his tribe; Gill offers the priestly ban on mourning or else impartiality in judgment; Keil and Wesley refer the words to the day the Levites drew the sword at Sinai

Whether Levi's blessing answers the Maccabees: Ellicott follows Rashi to the Asmonaean war and notes that Mattathias was a priest of the sons of Joiarib, and Gill reports Jarchi to the same effect, where Clarke reads the blessing on the substance economically, as following the fertility of the land
outliers: Calvin's account of the blessing as a deliberate modification of Jacob's harsher sentence, made for the whole people's sake rather than the tribe's
Calvin's application to pastors, that they must put off the earthly affections which would keep them from devoting themselves entirely to God
Clarke's derivation of Urim as all light and wisdom and Thummim as all excellence and perfection from Christ
Clarke's economic argument that the more fruitful the land, the more abundant the tithes, so Levi's substance grows with Israel's
Gill's note that some render the word for substance as a host or army, their service being a warfare
Henry's observation that Holiness to the Lord was written on the high priest's forehead in token of his holy office
Keil's remark that Levi proved itself holy although in the latter trial Moses and Aaron themselves stumbled

12.pericope_label: Benjamin between his shoulders, and the precious things of Joseph

schools.summary: Gill says the tribe of Benjamin is taken notice of next to Levi because, as the priesthood was in the tribe of Levi, the temple in which the priests officiated was in the tribe of Benjamin, or near it; and it is observed next but one to Judah, and before his elder brother Joseph, because his tribe lay between Judah and Joseph, Levi having no inheritance in the land. Of the sun he quotes Jarchi, that the land of Joseph lay open to the sun and it sweetened the fruits of it, improving them and making them more valuable; and he adds that this is spiritually true of Christ the sun of righteousness, to whose influence are owing the blessings of grace, redemption, peace, pardon and justification, and the graces of the Spirit. Of the ancient mountains he says they were from the beginning of the world, and that the land possessed by the children of Joseph was famous for them, as the mountains of Gilead and Bashan inherited by Manasseh and Mount Ephraim and the mountains of Samaria by Ephraim, which produced, besides great quantities of grass and corn, also vines, figs and olives. Of the precious things of the earth he names corn of all sorts, the grass that grows out of it and the cattle that feed upon it, for all which some part of the land of Joseph, particularly Bashan, was famous, both for its oaks and for its pasturage. Of the bullock he says such were in Bashan, a country possessed by the posterity of Joseph, and so might be called his bullock; a young bull was reckoned both comely and majestic, and Gill cites the report that Menis or Mnevis, king of Egypt, preferred a bull above all animals to be worshipped as the most beautiful of all, and that Astarte put a bull's head upon her own as a sign of kingly power. Calvin says it is probable that Moses alludes to the inheritance which fell to the lot of the children of Benjamin, for the part of Jerusalem in which the temple stood was contained in it; since therefore God assigned them a dwelling-place in which he in a manner protected them and cherished them beneath his wings, they are not without reason called his, for this was no ordinary pledge of his love. To dwell upon God and between his shoulders, Calvin says, is equivalent to reposing upon him, a similitude taken from fathers who carry their children whilst yet they are small and tender; others, he notes, extract a different meaning. Of Joseph he says Moses repeats some portions of the blessing of Jacob, nor with respect to any other tribe does he approach so closely to the words of the Patriarch; and although the family of Joseph was already divided into two tribes or nations, still he begins by the head itself, and at the conclusion declares that what had been given to their fathers pertains to Ephraim and Manasseh. First he celebrates the exceeding fertility of the land in which the descendants of Joseph were to dwell, and then ratifies his testimony by the authority of God. Of the mountains Calvin says that in these words Moses shows that no part of the land would be barren: we know that the tops of mountains are generally uncultivated, or at any rate bear nothing but trees that have no fruit, but Moses affirms that even there also there shall be the richest produce; and their antiquity is not praised as if they were created before the rest of the world. Of the bullock he says translators obscure the meaning by rendering the word in the nominative case, and that he has no doubt Moses compares the glory of Joseph to the size of a very fine bullock, as if he had said, his beauty is as of the most choice bullocks in his herds, so that no more magnificent or glorious bullocks should be found in the land of Joseph than the people itself would be; and to beauty he adds strength and vigour.

Henry says Benjamin is put next to Levi because the temple, where the priests' work lay, was just upon the edge of the lot of this tribe; and it is put before Joseph because of the dignity of Jerusalem, part of which was in this tribe, above Samaria, which was in the tribe of Ephraim, and because Benjamin adhered to the house of David and to the temple of the Lord when the rest of the tribes deserted both with Jeroboam. Benjamin is here called the beloved of the Lord, Henry notes, and the father of this tribe was Jacob's beloved son, the son of his right hand; those are blessed indeed who are beloved of the Lord.

Clarke says the title alludes to Benjamin's being particularly beloved of his father Jacob, and that he shall dwell in safety by the Lord, whose temple, considered as his dwelling-place, was in the tribe of Benjamin, since a part of Jerusalem belonged to this tribe; he shall cover him all the day means, be his continual protector, and he shall dwell between his shoulders means within his coasts, or in his chief city, Jerusalem, where the temple of God was built on his mountains Zion and Moriah, here poetically termed his shoulders; some, Clarke notes, object to this translation of the Hebrew. Of Joseph he says the whole passage certainly relates to the peculiar fertility of the soil in the portion that fell to this tribe, which the Jews say yielded a greater abundance of all good things than any other part of the promised land: the precious things of heaven are the peculiar mildness and salubrity of its atmosphere; the dew, a plentiful supply of which was a great blessing in the dry soil of a hot climate; and the deep that coucheth beneath probably refers to the plentiful supply of water which should be found in digging wells, whence the Septuagint has fountains of the deep. The precious fruits brought forth by the sun are all excellent and important productions of the earth which come to perfection once in the year, so the precious things put forth by the moon may imply those vegetables which require but about a month to bring them to perfection, or vegetables of which several crops may be had in the course of a year. The chief things of the ancient mountains probably refers to the large trees growing on the mountain tops and the springs of water issuing from them, the mountains of Gilead perhaps being intended, as they fell to the half tribe of Manasseh, while the precious things of the lasting hills may signify the metals and minerals in them. The good will of him that dwelt in the bush means the favour of him who appeared in the burning bush on Mount Sinai, who there in his good will, mere love and compassion, took Israel to be his people, and who has preserved and will preserve, in tribulation and distress, all those who trust in him, so that they shall as surely escape unhurt as the bush, though enveloped with fire, was unburnt. Of the bullock Clarke says the similitude is very obscure: a bullock was the most excellent of animals among the Jews, not only because of its acceptableness in sacrifice but because of its great usefulness in agriculture, and there is something peculiarly noble and dignified in the appearance of the ox, whose greatest ornament are his fine horns, which the inspired penman has particularly in view, as the following clause proves. Wesley says Benjamin is put next to Levi because the temple, where the work of the Levites lay, was upon the edge of the lot of this tribe, and before Joseph because of the dignity of Jerusalem above Samaria, and because Benjamin adhered to the house of David and to the temple of God when the rest of the tribes deserted both. The beloved of the Lord is so called in allusion to their father Benjamin, who was the beloved of his father Jacob, and because of the kindness of God to this tribe. Of Joseph he says the name includes both Ephraim and Manasseh, and that in Jacob's blessing that of Joseph is the largest, and so it is here: his portion shall be endowed with choice blessings from God, the things of heaven being the precious fruits of the earth brought forth by the influences of heaven, the warmth of the sun and the rain which God will send; the deep means the springs of water bubbling out of the earth, and perhaps also the great deep, the abyss of waters supposed to be contained in the earth. The sun opens and warms the earth, cherishes and improves and in due time ripens the seeds and fruits of it, while the moon by its moisture refreshes and promotes them, the Hebrew having of the moons, or months, that is, which it bringeth forth in the several months or seasons of the year. The chief things of the ancient mountains are the excellent fruits, as grapes, olives and figs, which delight in mountains, or the precious minerals contained in them, called ancient and lasting as having been from the beginning of the world and likely to continue to the end of it, in opposition to those hills or mounts which have been cast up by man. The good will means all other effects of the good will and kindness of God, who not long since did for a time dwell or appear in the bush to Moses in order to the relief of his people. Of the bullock Wesley says it is a young bull, a stately creature, formerly used as an emblem of royal majesty, and that this seems to note the kingdom which Ephraim should obtain in Jeroboam and his successors; his horns mean that his strength and power shall be very great, and the people are all that shall oppose him, particularly the Canaanites; and though Manasseh be now more numerous, yet Ephraim shall shortly outstrip him.

Ellicott says it is generally agreed that the blessing of Benjamin points to the site of the place which Jehovah chose out of all the tribes of Israel, Jerusalem, in the tribe of Benjamin, and divides the Hebrew thus: unto Benjamin he said, beloved of Jehovah, he, that is Jehovah, will dwell in security upon him, covering him over all the day, and between his shoulders, that is his mountain slopes, he hath taken up his abode. Of Joseph he says the remark of Rashi is especially applicable here, that thou wilt find in the case of all the tribes that the blessing of Moses is drawn from the fountain of the blessing of Jacob; and as the voice of Judah, the office of Levi and the situation of Benjamin are singled out for notice, so the land of Joseph is blessed. Of the deep that coucheth beneath he quotes Rashi again, that the deep ascends in vapour and also gives moisture from below; and of the next verse, that the increase of the sun and the precious things put forth from month to month, or by night when the moon rules, are next alluded to. The good will of him that dwelt in the bush, Ellicott says, is a blessing peculiar to Moses, and contains an exquisite piece of interpretation: from the fact that Jehovah revealed himself to Moses in a flame of fire in a bush, the man of God drew the thought that he presented himself as dwelling in it, and thus he has furnished God's Church with this comfort for all ages, that his human temple, although it burn with fire, can never be consumed; the last part of the verse is taken direct from Genesis. Of the ten thousands of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh he says Rashi refers this to the ten thousands slain by Joshua, the Ephraimite leader, and the thousands slain by Gideon, who was of the tribe of Manasseh, expounding nearly the whole verse in reference to Joshua and the conquest of Canaan; and there is an obvious similarity, Ellicott adds, in the song of the Israelitish women after the defeat of the Philistines, that Saul hath slain his thousands and David his ten thousands. Keil renders the blessing of Joseph thus: blessed of the Lord be his land, of the most precious things of heaven, the dew, and of the flood which lies beneath, and of the most precious of the produce of the sun, and of the most precious of the growth of the moons, and of the head of the mountains of olden time, and of the most precious thing of the everlasting hills, and of the most precious thing of the earth and its fulness, and of the good will of him that dwelt in the bush; let the blessing come upon the head of Joseph and upon the top of the head of him that was separated from his brethren.

debates: What between his shoulders means: Clarke takes the shoulders for the mountains of the chief city, poetically so called, Ellicott for the mountain slopes on which Jehovah takes up his abode, and Calvin for a posture of repose, a similitude taken from fathers carrying their small children, while granting that others read it otherwise

Why Benjamin is placed between Judah and Joseph: Gill gives the temple's nearness and the tribe's position on the map, where Henry and Wesley add the dignity of Jerusalem above Samaria and Benjamin's adherence to the house of David and the temple when the rest deserted both with Jeroboam

How far Moses' blessing depends on Jacob's: Ellicott quotes Rashi for the general rule that in every tribe the blessing of Moses is drawn from the fountain of Jacob's, where Calvin restricts the closeness to Joseph alone, saying that with respect to no other tribe does Moses approach so closely to the patriarch's words

What the ten thousands and thousands are: Ellicott follows Rashi to the ten thousands slain by Joshua the Ephraimite and the thousands by Gideon of Manasseh, comparing the women's song over Saul and David, where Wesley reads the horns of the kingdom Ephraim would obtain under Jeroboam and Calvin of the people's own strength and vigour
outliers: Calvin's correction of the translators, who obscure the bullock by putting the word in the nominative case
Calvin's observation that mountain tops are usually barren or bear only fruitless trees, yet here are promised the richest produce
Clarke's inference that the Septuagint's fountains of the deep points to water found in digging wells
Ellicott's account of the bush as an exquisite piece of interpretation, comforting the Church that its human temple, though it burn, can never be consumed
Gill's report from Jarchi that the land of Joseph lay open to the sun, which sweetened its fruits
Rashi's note, quoted by Ellicott, that the deep ascends in vapour and also gives moisture from below
Wesley's distinction of ancient and lasting hills from those cast up by man

18.pericope_label: Zebulun and Issachar, and the enlarging of Gad

schools.summary: Gill says the tribe of Zebulun has Issachar joined with it, they being brethren and of the same mother as well as father, though Zebulun the youngest is set before Issachar the older, as in Jacob's blessing. Of the calling to the mountain he says the Targums make it the mountain of the house of the sanctuary, the temple built on a mountain, which Moses by a spirit of prophecy foresaw; to this the tribes of Zebulun and Issachar would not only come up themselves, though at the more distant parts of the land, but would call and urge others, both Israelites and Gentiles, to do the same, partly by their example and partly by persuasions and arguments, not only the tribes of Israel nearest them but the heathen, the Tyrians and others. Of Gad's portion he says it is the land of Sihon and Og, as Jarchi rightly interprets it, which was the beginning or firstfruits of the subduing of the land that was promised; this Gad looked at, chose and desired as his inheritance. Calvin says Moses compares two tribes with each other which, although neighbours in position, were still very dissimilar: the one, being devoted to mercantile pursuits, went forth frequently in various directions, while the other took more delight in quietude and repose, and this their great variety of condition is indicated when he bids Zebulun rejoice in its expeditions and Issachar in its domestic repose. Moses thus confirms the prophecy of Jacob, who said that Zebulun should dwell at the haven of the sea so as to make voyages of traffic, whilst Issachar delighted in quiet. In the blessing of the tribe of Gad, Calvin says, mention is only made of the hereditary portion which it had obtained without casting of lots; he therefore celebrates the blessing of God because he had accorded to the Gadites an ample dwelling-place, the word enlargeth referring to the extent of their possession. But inasmuch as in that extremity of the land beyond Jordan they were on a hostile border, he declares that they would be warlike, and hence compares them to a lion, which tears its prey sometimes from the head and sometimes from the arm. Of the first part Calvin says others translate it not badly, though Jerome's rendering is quite out of the question; the word is very suitable, for Moses thus signifies that the Gadites were beforehand in seeking a dwelling-place for themselves, since before possession of the land was accorded to the people they asked for the kingdom of Sihon for themselves.

Henry says the blessings of Zebulun and Issachar are put together, for they were both the sons of Jacob by Leah, and by their lot in Canaan they were neighbours. It is foretold that they should both have a comfortable settlement and employment: Zebulun must rejoice, for he shall have cause to rejoice, and Moses prays that he may have cause in his going out, either to war, for Zebulun jeoparded their lives in the high places of the field, or rather to sea, for Zebulun was a haven of ships; and Issachar must rejoice in his tents.

Clarke says rejoice, Zebulun, in thy going out means, thou shalt be very prosperous in thy coasting voyages, for this tribe's situation was favourable for traffic, having many sea-ports; and Issachar in thy tents means that, as Zebulun should be prosperous in his shipping and traffic, so should Issachar be in his tents, his agriculture and pasturage. Of the calling to the mountain he says that by their traffic with the Gentiles, for so he thinks the word should be understood here, they shall be the instruments in God's hands of converting many to the true faith, so that instead of sacrificing to idols they should offer sacrifices of righteousness. To suck of the abundance of the seas is to grow wealthy by merchandise; and of treasures hid in the sand, Clarke says, Jonathan ben Uzziel has probably hit upon the true meaning of this difficult passage, that from the sand are produced looking-glasses, that is, glass. Of Gad he says that, as deliverance out of distress is termed enlarging, this may refer to God's deliverance of the tribe of Gad out of the distress mentioned in Genesis, and to the enlargement obtained through Jephthah, and probably also to the victories obtained by Gad and Reuben over the Hagarites; and the epithet of lion was probably applied to this tribe from their fierce and warlike disposition. Of the first part he says Gad chose for himself a very excellent portion, the land of Sihon and Og, in which this tribe had requested to be settled by the lawgiver, that is by Moses, from whom they requested it; and notwithstanding this portion fell unto them on the east side of Jordan, yet they proceeded with the heads of the people, the chiefs of the other tribes, to execute the justice of the Lord, that is, to extirpate the old inhabitants of the country according to the divine decree. Wesley says rejoice means, thou shalt prosper and have cause of rejoicing, and in thy going out means to war, as the phrase is often used, or to sea in way of traffic, because their portion lay near the sea; in both respects his course is opposite to that of Issachar, who was a lover of peace and pasturage. He is joined with Zebulun both because they were brethren by father and mother and because their possessions lay near together; and in thy tents means, thou shalt give thyself to the management of land and cattle, living quietly in thy own possessions. Of the calling Wesley says it is Zebulun of whom Moses takes more special notice, so that having dispatched Issachar in two words he returns to Zebulun; the people are the Gentiles, either those of Galilee, which was called Galilee of the Gentiles and were their neighbours, or people of other nations with whom they had commerce, which they endeavoured to improve in persuading them to worship the true God; the mountain is the temple, which Moses knew was to be seated upon a mountain; and sacrifices of righteousness are such as God requires. Of Gad he says enlargeth means, that bringeth him out of his straits amid the troubles he was often engaged in, because he was encompassed with potent enemies; as a lion means safe and secure from his enemies and terrible to them when they rouse and molest him; and teareth the arm means he utterly destroys his enemies, both the head, the seat of the crown, their dignity and principality, and the arm, the subject of strength and instrument of action, both chief princes and their subjects. The first part is the firstfruits of the land of promise, the country of Sihon, which was first conquered, said to be provided for himself because he desired and obtained it of Moses; and of the lawgiver means of Moses, whose portion this is called, either because this part of the land beyond Jordan was the only part of the land which Moses was permitted to enter upon, or because it was given him by Moses, whereas the portions beyond Jordan were given to the several tribes by Joshua according to the direction of the lot.

Keil renders the blessing, rejoice, Zebulun, at thy going out, and, Issachar, at thy tents; nations will they invite to the mountain, there offer the sacrifices of righteousness, for they suck the affluence of the seas and the hidden treasures of the sand. The tribes of the last two sons of Leah Moses unites together, and, like Jacob, places Zebulun the younger first, first of all confirming the blessing which Jacob pronounced. Of Gad he renders, blessed be he that enlargeth Gad: like a lioness he lieth down and teareth the arm, yea, the crown of the head; and he chose his first-fruit territory, for there was the leader's portion kept, and he came with the heads of the people, he executed the justice of the Lord and his judgments with Israel. Ellicott says Zebulun and Issachar were united with Judah in the leading division of Israel in the wilderness, and that the warlike character of the first of these two and the more peaceful wisdom of the second are illustrated by the song of Deborah and by the men of Issachar who had understanding of the times. Of the calling he renders, they shall give the mountain-call to the peoples, that is, they shall call the tribes of Israel to Mount Moriah to offer the sacrifices of righteousness, citing the passover of Hezekiah for an illustration. Of Gad he says the mountains of Gilead shut him in, and cites the eleven Gadites whose faces were as the faces of lions. Of the first part he says the first territory conquered by Moses was distributed between Reuben and Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh; a portion of the lawgiver is interpreted by Rashi as the field of the burial-place of the lawgiver, but this, Ellicott says, can hardly have been in the mind of Moses. He came with the heads of the people means that the Gadites with their companion tribes passed over Jordan to the conquest of Canaan by Moses' order.

debates: Whom Zebulun and Issachar call to the mountain: Ellicott keeps it inside Israel, taking it of calling the tribes to Mount Moriah, where Clarke reads the word of the Gentiles reached through trade and made converts to the true faith, Wesley names them as the men of Galilee or the nations they traded with, and Gill will have both Israelites and heathen

What the portion of the lawgiver is: Ellicott reports Rashi's reading of it as the field of Moses' burial-place and answers that this can hardly have been in Moses' mind; Wesley offers either the only part of the land Moses was allowed to enter or the part he himself assigned, as against the lots cast by Joshua; Calvin rejects Jerome's rendering outright and takes the clause of the Gadites' forwardness in asking for Sihon's kingdom first

What enlarging Gad means: Clarke takes it of deliverance out of distress, pointing to Jephthah and the victories over the Hagarites, where Calvin refers it to the extent of the possession itself and Wesley to being brought out of straits amid troubles

What the treasures hid in the sand are: Clarke calls the passage difficult and thinks Jonathan ben Uzziel has probably hit the sense in the glass produced from that sand, while Keil renders it plainly as hidden treasures and Gill and Wesley take the whole clause of wealth got by trade
outliers: Calvin's explanation of Gad's warlike character from his position on a hostile border beyond Jordan
Clarke's report of Jonathan ben Uzziel that from the sand are produced looking-glasses
Ellicott's note that the mountains of Gilead shut Gad in
Ellicott's citation of the eleven Gadites whose faces were as the faces of lions
Henry's observation that Zebulun jeoparded their lives in the high places of the field, yet was also a haven of ships
Keil's note that Moses, like Jacob before him, places Zebulun the younger before Issachar the elder
Wesley's reading of tearing the arm and the crown as destroying both chief princes and their subjects

22.pericope_label: Dan, Naphtali and Asher: the lion, the favour, and the iron shoes

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem take each of these in turn of the tribe, of Dan, of Naphtali and of Asher. Of the shoes of iron and brass he says either they should have such an abundance of these metals that they could, if they would, have made their shoes of them, though that is not usual, and it is said of Empedocles the philosopher that he wore shoes of brass, which was very singular; or that this tribe, because of the abundance of these metals, used to stud their shoes with iron and brass nails at the bottom of them, as country people, soldiers and travellers in various nations do; but the true sense, Gill says, seems to be that it describes the land that fell to this tribe. Calvin foretells that the tribe of Dan, like that of Gad, should be warlike, not so much from voluntary disposition as from necessity, for their love of war was not to be deemed praiseworthy, inasmuch as it is altogether contrary to humanity, but because the unscrupulousness of the enemies by which that tribe was infested compelled them to take up arms. He compares it to a lion impetuously leaping from Mount Bashan, and the particle of comparison must be understood here, Calvin says, for Mount Bashan was not situated in the territory of this tribe. Of Naphtali he predicts that God would deal bountifully towards these two tribes, since to the first a fertile district would be allotted towards the west and the south. What Moses declares respecting the tribe of Asher, Calvin says, is not free from ambiguity, for he is said to be blessed with a word which may mean either children or something else: if we prefer the former meaning, his prolificness is celebrated, as though it were said, Asher shall be blessed with a numerous progeny; there may, however, be a comparison between this tribe and the others.

Henry says Jacob in his blessing had compared Dan to a serpent for subtlety, while Moses compares him to a lion for courage and resolution; and what could stand before those that had the head of a serpent and the heart of a lion? He is compared to the lions that leaped from Bashan, a mountain noted for fierce lions, whence they came down to leap upon their prey in the plains; and this may refer to the particular victories obtained by Samson, who was of this tribe, over the Philistines. Of the closing promise Henry says all shall be sanctified to true believers: if their way be rough, their feet shall be shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace. The day is often in Scripture put for the events of the day, so that as thy days so shall thy strength be is a promise that God would graciously and constantly support under trials and troubles, whatever they were; it is a promise sure to all the spiritual seed of Abraham. Have they work allotted? They shall have strength to do it. Have they burdens appointed? They shall have strength, and never be tempted above what they are able to bear.

Clarke says the Jewish interpreters observe that Bashan was a place much frequented by lions, who issued thence into all parts to look for prey, and that by this Moses probably intended to point out the strength and prowess of the tribe of Dan, that it should extend its territories and live a sort of predatory life; it appears that the portion originally assigned to this tribe was not sufficient for them, hence we find them going out to war against Leshem and taking it and adding it to their territories. Of Naphtali he says that, though the words may refer to the very great fertility of the country that fell to this tribe, certainly something more is intended: scarcely any of the tribes was more particularly favoured by the wondrous mercy and kindness of God than this and the tribe of Zebulun, since the light of the glorious Gospel of Christ shone brightly here, Christ's chief residence being at Capernaum in this tribe. Of Asher he says, let him have a numerous posterity, continually increasing; let him be acceptable to his brethren, in perfect union and harmony with the other tribes; and let him dip his foot in oil, that is, let him have a fertile soil and an abundance of all the conveniences and comforts of life. Of the shoes he says some suppose the words may refer to the iron and copper mines in their territory, but it is more likely that they relate to their warlike disposition, since greaves, boots and shoes of iron, brass and tin were used by ancient warriors: Goliath had greaves of brass on his legs, and the brazen-booted Greeks is one of the epithets Homer gives his heroes. Wesley says a lion's whelp means courageous and generous and strong and successful against his enemies, and which leapeth from Bashan because there were many and fierce lions in those parts; this may refer either to the particular victories obtained by Samson, who was of the tribe of Dan, or to a more general achievement of that tribe, when a party of them surprised Laish, which lay in the farthest part of the land of Canaan from them, the mountain of Bashan lying not far from that city. Of Naphtali he says, satisfied with favour, that is, with the favour of God: that only is the favour that satisfies the soul, and they are happy indeed that have the favour of God, and they shall have it that place their satisfaction in it. Full with the blessing of the Lord means not only with corn, wine and oil, the fruit of the blessing, but with the blessing itself, the grace of God according to his promise and covenant; and possess thou the west and the south, or the sea and the south, is not to be understood of the place, that his lot should fall there. Of Asher, who carries blessedness in his very name, he says, be blessed with children, that is, he shall have numerous, strong and healthful children; acceptable to his brethren by his sweet disposition and winning carriage; and in oil, so that he shall have such plenty of oil that he may not only wash his face but his feet also in it. The iron and brass are the mines of iron and copper which were in their portion, whence Sidon their neighbour was famous among the heathens for its plenty of brass, and Sarepta is thought to have its name from the brass and iron which were melted there in great quantity; and thy strength shall be means, thy strength shall not be diminished with age, but thou shalt have the vigour of youth even in thine old age, and thy tribe shall grow stronger and stronger.

Ellicott says Jacob compared Dan to a serpent and an adder, and that the lion of the tribe of Dan is not like the lion of the tribe of Judah; the leaping from Bashan probably refers to the taking of Laish, which was a sudden, treacherous surprise, like the spring of a lion on his prey. He notes that the hill of Bashan is opposed to God's hill in the Psalms, that the kine of Bashan are reproved in Amos, and that the bulls of Bashan represent the enemies of Christ. Of Asher he says the words can be translated, more blessed than all sons, and quotes Rashi's old saying, that you will not find among all the tribes one so blest with children as Asher, and I cannot say why; the fertility of Asher's inheritance is probably alluded to in the dipping of the foot in oil. There is no tribe of which so little is recorded in history, Ellicott adds, and the happiest lives are sometimes the least eventful. Of the shoes he says perhaps we should rather read, thy bars shall be iron and brass, since the word here rendered shoes in the Authorised Version does not occur elsewhere and the nearest word to it means locks or fastenings; it is also uncertain whether the whole sentence belongs to the blessing of Asher or to all Israel, though it seems most likely that, as Asher's territory was at the northern end of Palestine, close to the pass by which the most formidable invaders must enter in, an assurance is here given concerning the frontier of Israel. Keil renders the blessing of Naphtali, O Naphtali, satisfied with favour and full of the blessing of Jehovah; of sea and south shall he take possession. If the gracefulness of Naphtali is set forth in the blessing of Jacob by comparing it to a gazelle, here Moses assures the same tribe of satisfaction with the favour and blessing of God and promises it the possession of the sea and of the south. Of Asher he renders, blessed before the sons be Asher; let him be the favoured among his brethren, and dipping his foot in oil; iron and brass be thy castle, and as the days of thy life let thy rest continue. Asher, the prosperous, was justly to bear the name, Keil says: he was to be a child of prosperity, blessed with earthly good and enjoying rest all his life long in strong fortresses. The conclusion of the blessing, he adds, corresponds to the introduction: as Moses commenced with the glorious fact of the founding of the kingdom of Jehovah in Israel, so he also concludes with a reference to the Lord their eternal refuge.

debates: Whether Asher is blessed with children or above them: Ellicott says the words can be rendered, more blessed than all sons, and quotes Rashi's saying that no tribe was so blest with children and he cannot say why; Keil renders, blessed before the sons; Calvin states the ambiguity plainly, that the word may celebrate his prolificness or set up a comparison with the other tribes; Clarke and Wesley take the children without hesitation

What the shoes of iron and brass are: Ellicott would read bars rather than shoes, since the word occurs nowhere else and the nearest to it means fastenings, and doubts whether the clause belongs to Asher or to all Israel; Clarke takes them for the greaves of ancient warriors, citing Goliath and Homer's brazen-booted Greeks; Wesley and Gill take the mines of the district, Gill also canvassing studded shoes and the brazen shoes of Empedocles

Whether Dan's warlikeness is praised: Calvin denies it, holding that their love of war was not praiseworthy, being altogether contrary to humanity, and that necessity rather than disposition drove them to arms, where Henry and Wesley take the lion as courage and resolution and Clarke as strength and prowess in a predatory life

What the leap from Bashan means: Ellicott and Wesley refer it to the surprise of Laish, Ellicott calling it sudden and treacherous, while Henry and Wesley also allow the victories of Samson, and Calvin insists the particle of comparison must be supplied since Bashan lay outside the tribe's territory
outliers: Calvin's judgment that a love of war is altogether contrary to humanity and not to be deemed praiseworthy
Clarke's citation of the brazen-booted Greeks, one of Homer's epithets for his heroes
Ellicott's remark that no tribe has so little recorded of it as Asher, and that the happiest lives are sometimes the least eventful
Gill's report that Empedocles the philosopher wore shoes of brass
Henry's question, what could stand before those that had the head of a serpent and the heart of a lion
Rashi's old saying, quoted by Ellicott, that no tribe was so blest with children as Asher, and I cannot say why
Wesley's rule that only the favour of God satisfies the soul, and that they shall have it who place their satisfaction in it

26.pericope_label: No God like the God of Jeshurun, and the everlasting arms

schools.summary: Gill says the Lord was Israel's God in a special sense, having chosen and redeemed them and made a covenant with them, and that there is no God like him for the perfections of his nature, his purity and holiness, goodness, wisdom, power and faithfulness, and for the wonderful works of nature, providence and grace done by him. Of the eternal God he says God is eternal, from everlasting to everlasting, the Ancient of days, before all things and all time; and the same is true of Christ, who is the everlasting Father, the true God and eternal life, as appears from his nature, having the whole fulness of deity in him, and from his office as Mediator, in which he was set up from everlasting. Of Israel dwelling alone he says the Canaanites being thrust out of their land and Israel put into possession of it, they should dwell in safety, or confidently, without fear of enemies, though surrounded by them on all hands, and though alone, a separate people distinct from all their neighbours; so the spiritual Israel dwell in the eternal God, their mansion or dwelling place, in Christ their rock, and in a strong city, the church, where they are in the utmost safety. The last verse Gill calls the conclusion of the blessing summed up in a few words: they had God to be their God and so many good things promised them and in sight of them, being now got through the wilderness and on the borders of Canaan; and all such must be happy whose covenant God is the Lord, since they must be beloved of him, chosen by him and blessed with all spiritual blessings. Calvin says Moses proceeds from the parts to the whole and now comes to speak of the whole body, which consisted of the twelve families; all that he says tends to the same end, that the people of Israel were happy as being taken by God under his faithful guardianship, for nothing is more to be desired with regard to our best interests than that our welfare should be entrusted to the hand of God. But since this inestimable blessing of being protected by the care of God is often but lightly prized, Moses exclaims in admiration that there is none to be compared with him. Of the refuge Calvin says it is just as if he had said that the Israelites were protected from above by the help of God and also based, as it were, upon him; the beginning of the prayer corresponds with that other in the ninetieth psalm, Lord, thou hast been our dwelling-place in all generations. The sum is that although the Israelites might be exposed to many injuries, still there was secure repose for them under the shadow of God's wings, and assuredly unless the hand of God had been like a roof to protect them they would have perished a thousand times over. Of Israel dwelling alone he says Moses promises to the elect people what all have naturally a great desire for, namely peace or tranquillity, for he is said to dwell confidently who fears no danger, whom no care harasses, and who needs no garrison or defence. This, indeed, God never vouchsafed altogether to the Israelites, Calvin says, that they should inhabit their land in security and without the fear of enemies, inasmuch as their ingratitude did not allow of it. Of the last verse he says Moses again exclaims that happy is the people whose salvation is in God, and surely this is the only true happiness, for unless we ascend to the first cause of salvation all salvations, so to speak, are but transitory; and by the shield and the sword is meant a perfect defence, as much as to say that no part of their armour was to be sought elsewhere.

Henry says these are the last words of all that ever Moses, that great writer, that great dictator, either wrote himself or had written from his dictation; they are therefore very remarkable, and no doubt we shall find them very improving. Moses, the man of God, who had as much reason as ever any mere man had to know both, with his last breath magnifies both the God of Israel and the Israel of God; they are both incomparable in his eye, and we are sure that in this his judgment of both his eye did not wax dim. There is no God like the God of Israel, Henry says: none of the gods of the nations can be compared with him.

Clarke says that besides the literal meaning of Jeshurun the word seems to be used as an expression of particular affection, so that Calmet understands it as a diminutive of the word Israel; and we know, he adds, that the Greek word for sons in the mouth of St John signifies much less than the word which, properly translated, would be beloved children, a term which at once shows the helplessness of the offspring and the tender affection of the parent, and so Jeshurun may be understood here. The eternal God, he says, means the former God, he who was of old, not like the gods which were lately come up, he who ever was and ever will be, and who was, is and will be unchangeably holy, wise, just and merciful; and as the arm is the emblem of power, and of power in a state of exertion, the everlasting arms state that an unlimited and unconquerable power shall be eternally exerted in the defence of God's Church and in behalf of all those who trust in him. Of Israel dwelling alone Clarke says this people shall not be incorporated with any other people under heaven, a prophecy which continues to be fulfilled to the very letter, since every attempt to unite them with any other people has proved absolutely ineffectual; and the fountain of Jacob, that is his offspring, shall possess a most fertile land, such as Palestine was. Of the last verse he exclaims, O the happiness of Israel: it is ineffable, inconceivable, because they are a people saved by the Lord, having such a salvation as it becomes the infinite perfections of God to bestow; he is their help, their never-failing strength, and the shield of that help, defending their defence, saving them and preserving them in the state of salvation. The sword of thy excellency means, or whose sword, his all-conquering Word, is thine excellency, in its promises, threatenings and precepts, and Clarke compares St Paul's exhortation to the Ephesians. Wesley says these are the last words that ever Moses wrote, perhaps the greatest writer that ever lived upon the earth, and that this man of God, who had as much reason to know both as ever any mere man had, with his last breath magnifies both the God of Israel and the Israel of God. Riding on the heaven denotes the greatness and glory in which God manifests himself to the upper world, and the use he makes of the influences of heaven. The eternal God is he who was before all worlds and will be when time shall be no more; thy refuge, or thy habitation or mansion-house, so the word signifies, in whom thou art safe and easy and at rest as a man is in his own house. Every true Israelite is at home in God, Wesley says: the soul returns to him and reposes in him, and they that make him their habitation shall have all the comforts and benefits of an habitation in him; and underneath are the everlasting arms, the almighty power of God, which protects and comforts all that trust in him. Of Israel dwelling alone he offers two senses: either though they be alone and have no confederates to defend them but have all the world against them, yet my single protection shall be sufficient for them; or, distinct and separated from all other nations, with whom I will not have them mingle themselves. The fountain is the posterity of Jacob, which flowed from him as waters from a fountain in great abundance, the fountain being here put for the river or streams which flow from it, as Jacob or Israel is often put for the children of Israel. Of the last verse Wesley says the shield of thy help means, by whom thou art sufficiently guarded against all assailants, and the sword of thy excellency, or thy most excellent sword, means thy strength and the author of all thy past or approaching victories; those in whose hearts is the excellency of holiness have God himself for their shield and sword, being defended by the whole armour of God, his word their sword and faith their shield. Thine enemies shall be found liars unto thee, he adds, who said they would destroy thee, or at least that they would never submit.

Keil renders the passage, who is as God, a righteous nation, who rides in heaven to thy help and in his exaltation upon the clouds; abiding is the God of olden time, and beneath are everlasting arms, and he drives the enemy before thee and says, Destroy.
