The meaning, he says, is that no other nation has a God who rules in heaven with almighty power and is a refuge and help to his people against every foe; Jeshurun is a vocative, and the alteration proposed on the authority of the ancient versions is to be rejected. Of the following verse he renders, and Israel dwells safely, alone the fountain of Jacob, in a land full of corn and wine; his heavens also drop down dew: because the God of old was the dwelling and help of Israel, it dwelt safely and separate from the other nations. Of the last verse he renders, hail to thee, O Israel, who is like thee, a people saved in the Lord, the shield of thy help, and who is the sword of thine eminence; thine enemies will deny themselves to thee, and thou ridest upon their heights. Saved, Keil insists, means not merely delivered from danger and distress but in general endowed with salvation. Ellicott sums the opening in the words, their rock is not as our Rock. Of the refuge he says the word thy is not represented in the original, and that the Hebrew word for refuge differs very slightly from the refuge of the ninetieth psalm, Lord, thou hast been our refuge in generation and generation, which are also the words of Moses; the same word is used of the habitation of Jehovah in heaven. Perhaps, he adds, we ought to connect this clause with what precedes and render the passage, there is none like the God of Jeshurun, riding on the heavens for thy help, and in his majesty on the sky, the dwelling of the God of old. Of Israel dwelling in safety he says it means in confidence and security, comparing the promise that in the days of Messiah Judah shall be saved and Israel shall dwell safely, but not until they learn to rest upon the everlasting arms. Of the enemies being found liars he compares the psalm which says that through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves, that is, lie, unto thee; the idea is that the enemies of the conqueror will hasten to throw themselves at his feet, protesting that they were always his friends, as Shimei did on the occasion of David's return to Jerusalem.

debates: Whether Israel dwelling alone was in fact fulfilled: Clarke says the prophecy continues to be fulfilled to the very letter, since every attempt to incorporate this people with another has proved absolutely ineffectual, while Calvin says God never vouchsafed it altogether to the Israelites, their ingratitude not allowing them to inhabit their land without fear of enemies, and Ellicott defers the promise to the days of Messiah

What dwelling alone means: Wesley offers both that they had no confederates and needed none, God's single protection sufficing, and that they were to be kept distinct from all other nations, with whom he would not have them mingle; Gill takes the word as confidence, dwelling without fear though surrounded on all hands

How the refuge should be construed: Ellicott notes that the pronoun thy is absent from the original and would perhaps join the clause to what precedes, reading it as the dwelling of the God of old, where Wesley presses the domestic sense of habitation or mansion-house and Calvin, like Ellicott, refers the word to the ninetieth psalm

What being found liars means: Ellicott takes it of enemies throwing themselves at the conqueror's feet and protesting they were always his friends, comparing Shimei at David's return, while Wesley refers the lie backward to their boast that they would destroy Israel or never submit
outliers: Calvin's image of the hand of God as a roof, without which they would have perished a thousand times over
Calvin's rule that unless we ascend to the first cause of salvation, all salvations are but transitory
Clarke's analogy from the Greek, that Jeshurun stands to Israel as beloved children to sons, showing the helplessness of the offspring and the tenderness of the parent
Clarke's gloss that the everlasting arms mean an unlimited power eternally exerted in the defence of God's Church
Henry's remark that in this last judgment of God and of Israel the eye of Moses did not wax dim
Keil's insistence that saved means not merely delivered from distress but endowed with salvation
Wesley's note that every true Israelite is at home in God, the soul returning to him and reposing in him
